blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en:
Language-model systems batch questions for throughput, but unrelated questions
should not change a target’s answer when its input and numerical execution
are fixed. We study compression of the key and value cache, which stores
attention representations reused during generation. With request-local groups,
Transformers’ Half-Quadratic Quantization (HQQ) backend updates compression
parameters separately but uses a shared average error to decide when all updates stop.
Replacing only the question batched with the target changes four-bit HQQ
answers in 170/384 test comparisons across two models. Replaying the
other execution’s update counts reproduces its complete answer and cache
fingerprints in every changed pair, in both directions. Computing the stopping
mean in FP32 reduces cache differences but leaves answer changes.
Native HQQ also changes confirmed numerical correctness in eight arithmetic pairs.
Fixed iterations and request-local stopping remove observed companion
dependence under matched controls. Request-local stopping remains sensitive to synthetic
padding changes at the tensor level. Fixing the original iteration budget removes this decision path
without tuning. Neither repair has an established
quality advantage, and natural rebatching still changes answers.
Request-independence audits must cover stopping decisions as well as
quantization groups.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Serving systems batch unrelated questions for efficiency, but a target’s answer
should not depend on other questions in its batch, called companions. Beyond
known floating-point effects ( Yuan et al., 2025 ; vLLM Project, 2026 ) , we test for dependence from cache
compression with target input, positions, attention mask, and padded batch shape fixed.

blocks.en:
The key and value (KV) cache stores attention representations reused during
generation. Quantization stores them as low-bit codes with reconstruction
parameters. Half-Quadratic Quantization (HQQ) iteratively fits these parameters ( Badri and Shaji, 2023 ) and is a cache backend in the Transformers model execution
library ( Wolf et al., 2020 ; Hugging Face, 2026 ) . Although quantization
groups and updates stay within each request, HQQ averages reconstruction error
across requests to decide when all updates stop. Companions can change the target’s update count.

blocks.en:
HQQ iteratively fits compression parameters without calibration data ( Badri and Shaji, 2023 ) . In Transformers’ HQQ cache integration, groups and
updates remain request-local, but the legacy optimizer averages errors across
requests to decide when all updates stop ( HQQ Contributors, 2026 ) .
Companions can thus change update counts. We reproduce changed answers by
replaying counts under matched computation and verify fixed or per-request
stopping as repairs. We check independence of termination as well as quantization parameters.

updates zero points using group-local means. It tests the earlier
reconstruction’s tensor-wide mean absolute error for strict improvement,

optimization of BF16 inputs. Fixed k k updates remove the shared test;
disabling optimization keeps initialization. Request-local stopping applies
the native test per request and freezes finished requests with masks.

questions. Five models give 960 model/question pairs. The test set contains 128
arithmetic questions from GSM8K’s official test split ( Cobbe et al., 2021 ) and 64 document-QA questions from HotpotQA’s official validation split with

disabled ( Yang et al., 2025 ) each answer all 192 test targets with two fixed
companions, giving 384 pairs.
The test set excludes earlier source IDs and normalized questions, including
those in the development set. HotpotQA also excludes document-title overlap
within the test set and with development inputs.
Appendix A gives models, prompts, companion selection,
revisions, and sampling restrictions.

blocks.en:
Local quantization groups do not ensure request separation when termination
is shared. Count replay under matched computation connects shared stopping
to complete answers with HQQ caches. Fixed iterations repair this dependence.
Request-local stopping preserves independent compression’s stopping behavior
on the same padded input, with no established practical advantage over fixed
iterations.

blocks.en: Limitations

blocks.en:
The controlled cache study uses two-request batches and a pinned HQQ legacy
optimizer in Transformers, with requests entering the same compression call. Requests sharing a GPU need not share a compression call, so GPU sharing
alone does not imply this dependence. The study does not establish how often
this configuration is deployed, failure in every HQQ backend, or information
disclosure.
The weight study extends the evaluation beyond KV caches, but uses the same
HQQ lineage rather than a second independent quantization mechanism. Its
controlled BF16 reconstruction does not evaluate an entire TorchAO runtime
or actual int4 inference kernels.

The causal intervention and the stored-record audit have different scopes.
Exact causal transfer is established for the 170 changed native-HQQ test
pairs and covers recorded runs through EOS or the fixed generation cap. The offline audit
checks the stored cache fingerprints, computed from contiguous FP32-converted
tensor representations; it does not independently recompute hidden states.

The preservation argument, in turn, assumes matched numerical execution.
Natural rebatching can change shapes and kernels, so the argument does not

is conditional on the fixed test questions and two models, assumes symmetric
seed-level differences, and compares only BF16, native HQQ and fixed 20.
It does not establish a population-level accuracy or serving benefit.
The FP32 generation ablation covers all test arithmetic questions but retains
only 16 input-selected QA questions per model; it reuses test inputs rather
than providing a new independent accuracy evaluation.

The unchanged final-number extractor leaves 20, 15, and 200 arithmetic pairs
with an unresolved side. Mistral has 181 unresolved answers in each native
condition: 169 of these in separate compression and 165 in joint compression
reach EOS, so missing recognized final-number assertions are not mainly a
length-cap effect. In each condition, 166 of the 181 unresolved outputs
contain the requested answer marker but fail the extractor’s accepted syntax.
For example, a marked number followed by “miles per hour” exceeds its
single-unit grammar; an empty marker supplies no number. Of the remaining
outputs, separate compression has 13 without recognized answer syntax and
two with unparsed answer clauses; joint compression has 15 without recognized
syntax. These automatic syntax categories explain extraction coverage without
assigning semantic correctness. The frozen extractor and scores are unchanged.
Unresolved answers are neither counted as wrong nor discarded. The coverage deficit prevents a general accuracy ranking; in
particular, Mistral’s BF16 count of 21 verified correct answers with 218
unresolved is not an estimate that only 21 answers are correct.

budget.

All 128 QA pairs have different initial reconstructed target-cache hashes,
with identical raw initial target inputs. In 127 of them the complete text
nevertheless stays unchanged. The low QA text-change count therefore does
not mean the compressor was unaffected. QA has one initial compression step
before the target ends and no later recompression. Math includes later
recompression in 240/256 Llama and 253/256 Qwen native answers. These counts
exclude compression events after the target has ended. They describe greater
exposure during longer generation, not an independent intervention on length.

blocks.en:
The weight study shows the same length contrast with an unquantized cache:
math medians are 216, 278 and 249 tokens for Llama, Qwen and Mistral; QA
medians are 5, 4.5 and 7. Math changes remain more frequent within the first
64 tokens (80/256, 99/256, 114/256) than QA changes (7/128, 6/128, 14/128).
Rolling cache recompression therefore cannot by itself explain the pattern
across both studies. Three Mistral QA answers reach the cap; all other native
QA answers in the weight study reach EOS. Prompts, task content, answer format,
length and model behavior remain confounded. More generation offers more
positions at which changed numerical states can affect the next token, but
these records do not identify how much of the task difference is caused by
length or establish that document grounding itself protects consistency.
